War Without a Vote

A week of unilateral strikes on Iran, a fired cabinet secretary, and a government still refusing to say who is watching whom

```markdown This was a week defined by a president who acted first and asked no one—not Congress, not the courts, not the public—and by the halting, often failed efforts of other institutions to catch up. It opened with strikes on Iran announced by video and closed with those strikes still underway, Congress having twice declined to reassert its own constitutional authority. In between, a cabinet secretary lost her job under bipartisan pressure, a court-ordered tariff refund gave way to a new tariff within days, and a private AI company found itself squeezed by the machinery of national-security law over a policy disagreement. Threaded through all of it were older, unresolved stories—Epstein-related testimony, election-integrity claims, protest restrictions—that moved without resolving.

**The Weekend.** It began with President Trump announcing military operations against Iran in a Truth Social video, calling for regime change and warning of a long conflict. The strikes proceeded even though Pentagon officials would later tell Congress there was no intelligence pointing to an imminent Iranian threat. Regional airspace closed and Iran's internet went dark within hours—consequences arriving before any public deliberation had occurred. The same weekend, the administration moved on a different front: after Anthropic refused Pentagon demands to loosen its AI safety guidelines, the Defense Department labeled the company a national-security supply-chain risk, a designation ordinarily reserved for foreign adversaries, and terminated its government contracts with the firm. Domestic frictions ran in parallel. A DHS memo instructed agents to flag naturalized citizens who had registered or voted before naturalization, reviving fears about noncitizen voting despite its rarity. The FBI searched Fulton County's election office over recycled 2020 fraud claims, and Los Angeles superintendent Alberto Carvalho was placed on leave after an FBI raid connected to a defunct ed-tech contractor—raising questions about whether the investigation was tied to his resistance to immigration enforcement near schools. Bill Clinton, meanwhile, testified for more than six hours before the House Oversight Committee on Epstein, the first former president compelled to testify under threat of contempt.

**Monday.** Trump confirmed the start of full combat operations, again bypassing ordinary channels, while Senator Tim Kaine and Representative Thomas Massie began pushing bipartisan war powers resolutions. The Pentagon's private assessment—that Iran had not been planning an unprovoked attack—stood in stark contrast to the administration's public rationale. New reporting added a further complication: Jared Kushner's firm had received Saudi and Emirati investment, and a Trump-branded development deal in Saudi Arabia was underway, even as both nations lobbied for military action against Iran. The financial entanglements did not prove motive, but they hung uncomfortably over a war launched without public debate. Florida lawmakers used the same day to advance a slate of bills criminalizing "foreign influence" political activity, restricting university funding tied to activism, empowering officials to designate groups as terrorist organizations, and creating a new state counterintelligence unit—a coordinated expansion of state power over dissent. In Washington, Senator Thom Tillis and colleagues grilled DHS Secretary Kristi Noem over the detention of American citizens, FEMA failures, and a $220 million advertising contract tied to a politically connected firm; Tillis called outright for her resignation. Courts, meanwhile, continued their quieter work, limiting DHS grant conditions on localities and protecting the *New York Times*' FOIA rights in a national-security case.

**Tuesday.** Two threads sharpened that would recur through the week. The House passed the SAVE America Act, 218-213, requiring proof of citizenship with documents matching a voter's current legal name—a technical requirement that could affect an estimated 69 million women who changed their names after marriage, with harsh penalties attached for election workers who err. And DHS's own inspector general told Congress that the department had refused to cooperate with a federal criminal investigation carrying national-security implications, part of a broader pattern of obstructed oversight. Noem faced renewed scrutiny before the Senate Judiciary Committee, refusing to retract her description of two Minnesotans killed by federal agents as "domestic terrorists" and denying enforcement quotas existed despite her own earlier public statements to the contrary. The Justice Department, days after signaling it would drop its defense of Trump's executive orders penalizing law firms tied to disfavored clients, abruptly reversed course and resumed the defense—a whiplash that suggested political pressure shaping litigation strategy. Separately, reporting surfaced that new Polymarket accounts had profited nearly a million dollars betting on a U.S. strike on Iran before it happened, while a fabricated war map had been used elsewhere to fake a Russian advance for betting gain, exposing how thinly regulated prediction markets can be exploited around matters of war.

**Wednesday.** The week brought its first formal reckoning on war powers. The Senate voted 47-53 against Kaine's resolution requiring congressional approval to continue military action, largely along party lines, leaving Trump free to proceed. The same day, a House Judiciary hearing turned up new discomfort for Noem: Trump had publicly contradicted her testimony that he personally approved the DHS ad campaign, and reports surfaced of internal turmoil tied to her relationship with a senior adviser. In Texas, a Republican-dominated state supreme court blocked a lower court's order extending primary voting hours in Dallas and Williamson counties amid widespread confusion over polling locations, ordering late ballots set aside rather than counted. The House Oversight Committee voted 24-19 to subpoena Attorney General Pam Bondi over the DOJ's handling of Epstein files, following the accidental release of survivors' names and unexplained redactions. And in a smaller but telling move, the DOJ opened an inquiry into former President Biden's use of an autopen, reportedly at Trump's own urging, without yet building any criminal case.

**Thursday.** The week's institutional consequences reached their conclusions. The House voted 212-219 against its own companion war powers resolution, following the Senate's rejection a day earlier—leaving both chambers, within 48 hours of each other, unwilling to reclaim authority the Constitution assigns to Congress. Kristi Noem was fired as DHS Secretary. After weeks of bipartisan criticism over the ad campaign, the Minnesota enforcement deaths, and contested testimony, Trump removed her and named Senator Markwayne Mullin as her replacement, effective at month's end; Noem was reassigned to a new envoy role. The change registered as a genuine break in personnel, but not in policy—the hardline enforcement approach that had drawn criticism showed no sign of softening under new leadership. The same day, a coalition of 24 states led by New York Attorney General Letitia James sued to block a new 15 percent tariff imposed under different statutory authority, arguing that Trump still lacked the power even after the Supreme Court had struck down his earlier "liberation day" tariffs. The administration escalated its pressure on Anthropic further, threatening to cut the company off from partners like Nvidia and Microsoft before abruptly shifting its own AI partnership to OpenAI. Elsewhere, a Haitian asylum seeker named Emmanuel Damas died in ICE custody of septic shock after staff failed to act on weeks of reported severe pain, and a gunman attacked a Dallas detention facility linked to ICE—two incidents, one of neglect and one of violence, both reflecting how volatile immigration enforcement had become. The DOJ also proposed a rule that would shield its own attorneys from state bar discipline pending internal review, even as Bondi separately directed staff to "zealously advance" the president's interests.

**Friday.** The week's loops closed, though rarely toward resolution. Trump reimposed 15 percent global tariffs under new legal authority just days after the Supreme Court's ruling against his earlier tariffs had forced refunds—refunds that Customs and Border Protection began processing at nearly the same moment the new tariffs took effect. Senator Richard Blumenthal opened a perjury investigation into Noem over whether she had misled Congress about adviser Corey Lewandowski's role in DHS contracting decisions. The White House ballroom project advanced despite overwhelming public opposition: the Commission of Fine Arts approved the $400 million plan to replace the East Wing, even as the National Capital Planning Commission postponed its own vote after receiving more than 35,000 comments, 97 percent opposed, and a federal judge declined to halt construction. Trump announced Mullin's appointment to succeed Noem via social media, ahead of any Senate confirmation process. Representative Tony Gonzales ended his re-election bid amid an ethics investigation tied to a past affair. CMS began migrating Medicare systems affecting 70 million Americans to Oracle's cloud platform, including generative AI tools, with little congressional scrutiny of the privacy implications. Kansas overrode its governor's veto to pass new anti-trans restrictions, and similar legislation advanced in Missouri, even as North Carolina primary voters rejected three anti-trans incumbents—a split verdict on the same underlying fight. The California State University system sued the Department of Education over Title IX conditions tied to a transgender athlete case, testing whether federal funding could be used to dictate university policy. And the DOJ quietly retreated from the autopen investigation into Biden, concluding there was no credible basis to proceed—a small instance of institutional resistance holding, even under direct presidential pressure.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government whose formal checks kept convening, arguing, and voting—and kept losing. Congress held hearings, drafted resolutions, and issued subpoenas, but failed twice on the one vote that would have reasserted its constitutional claim over war. Courts continued to rule against the executive on trade power, only to watch the same authority reassembled under a different statute within days. A cabinet secretary was removed under real bipartisan pressure, yet the policies she oversaw continued unaltered under her successor. Private companies, universities, and law firms found themselves treated as instruments to be pressured rather than institutions to be persuaded. None of this occurred through any single dramatic rupture; it accumulated through ordinary mechanisms—hearings, memos, contract terminations, court filings—each individually explicable, collectively describing a system straining to hold executive power accountable and, this week at least, not quite managing to. ```
